title: Helgoland to Farm Hall: the Uncertainty of Werner Heisenberg
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Würzburg to Munich: A Bavarian Education

stops.name: Würzburg, the professor's house
stops.campa: Werner Karl Heisenberg is born in Würzburg on 5 December, second son of August Heisenberg, a gymnasium teacher of Greek soon to become Germany's first professor of Byzantine studies, and Annie Wecklein, whose own father had headed Munich's Maximiliansgymnasium. Within the decade the family follows August's new chair to Munich, and the household is bookish, competitive, disciplined: the two brothers spar over chess and grades at the dinner table with a fierceness their father encourages, a training in argument the younger boy will carry whole into physics.
suggested_refs: Birth register of Würzburg, 5 December 1901
August Heisenberg's chair in Byzantine Studies, University of Munich
sources: David C. Cassidy, Uncertainty: The Life and Science of Werner Heisenberg (1992)

stops.name: Munich, the Maximiliansgymnasium
stops.campa: At the Maximiliansgymnasium, the same Munich school his own grandfather once headed, Heisenberg proves a formidable pupil, impatient with rote memorization but hungry for structure: he works through the calculus from a library book before his teachers reach it, and wrestles privately with Plato's Timaeus, drawn to the notion that the smallest constituents of matter must be shaped by mathematical law, geometry standing behind mere appearance. Music absorbs him too; he practices piano with the same ferocity he brings to a proof, and will play Beethoven sonatas his whole life for the discipline of it.
suggested_refs: Maximiliansgymnasium München
Plato's Timaeus, the schoolboy's private reading

stops.name: Munich, the war years and the school garden
stops.campa: The Great War empties Munich's shops and thins its bread; schoolboys are set to dig the Maximiliansgymnasium's grounds into potato plots and sent in summer to labor on Bavarian farms in place of the conscripted men. Heisenberg, thin and hungry like everyone, discovers in the privation a taste for hard physical work and open country that will never leave him; decades later, in the mountains and in his own theory of turbulence alike, he returns to this same appetite for wrestling something recalcitrant into order with his own hands.
suggested_refs: Wartime ration cards and school garden plots, Munich, 1916-1918

stops.name: Munich, the Freikorps and the fall of the Räterepublik
stops.campa: In the spring, Munich itself becomes a battlefield: a short-lived Bavarian Soviet Republic holds the city until Freikorps units and regular troops storm in from the south and west, house to house, in the first days of May. Heisenberg, not yet eighteen, serves as a dispatch runner for a student company attached to one of the government units, carrying messages through streets still under fire from rooftop machine guns. He will say little of it afterward, one soldier's-eye fragment among many in a Germany that has just lost a war and is now losing its own capitals to itself.
suggested_refs: Photographs of the May 1919 fighting in Munich, Bavarian Soviet Republic archive

stops.name: The Bavarian Alps, camps of the Neupfadfinder
stops.campa: That same year Heisenberg throws himself into the Pfadfinder scouting movement, and is soon elected leader of his own troop of younger boys drawn from his old student company. Nearly every free week for the next decade and more he takes them into the mountains around the Walchensee and beyond, tramping, camping under canvas, reading Goethe and the Greeks around the fire, singing. It is a romantic, disciplined, faintly nationalist fellowship of the outdoors, and it is here, on scree and rock face, that he first learns the particular joy of an unyielding problem solved by patience and nerve.
suggested_refs: Bund Deutscher Neupfadfinder troop photographs, Bavarian Alps, 1920s

stops.name: Munich, Sommerfeld's seminar
stops.campa: Heisenberg enters the University of Munich meaning to study pure mathematics, but a blunt rejection from Ferdinand Lindemann sends him instead to Arnold Sommerfeld, whose seminar in theoretical physics is already famous for the physicists it produces. Sommerfeld recognizes the nineteen-year-old's gift within weeks and, unusually, sets him at once on live research problems in the still-broken old quantum theory rather than years of exercises. Here Heisenberg meets Wolfgang Pauli, a year ahead of him and instantly a rival and friend, and the two argue physics late into Munich nights.
suggested_refs: Sommerfeld's Munich seminar room, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität

segments.name: Göttingen and Copenhagen: the Young Theorist

stops.name: Göttingen, the Bohr Festival
stops.campa: Sommerfeld brings his twenty-year-old student to Göttingen for the 'Bohr Festival', a fortnight of lectures in which Niels Bohr lays out his theory of the atom to the assembled physicists of Germany. After the third lecture Heisenberg rises, unafraid, to challenge a point in Bohr's argument from the floor; rather than take offense, Bohr invites him to walk and talk it through on the Hainberg hill outside town. Heisenberg will later call that walk the true beginning of his physics: the moment the older man's living, exploratory way of thinking about the atom became his own.
suggested_refs: The Hainberg hill above Göttingen, site of the walk with Bohr

stops.name: Göttingen, under Max Born
stops.campa: When Sommerfeld departs for a year's guest professorship in the United States, he sends Heisenberg to Göttingen to continue under Max Born, whose rigor in mathematical physics complements Sommerfeld's intuition. Born is at first uncertain what to make of the restless, self-assured young man dropped into his group, but sets him to work on the quantum theory of helium and the vexed problem of anomalous atomic spectra. In this Göttingen year, arguing daily with Born and with Pascual Jordan, Heisenberg's instinct hardens: the old theory's borrowed classical pictures of orbits must eventually be thrown away entirely.
suggested_refs: Max Born's Göttingen institute, Bunsenstrasse

stops.name: Munich, the doctoral exam and Wien's fury
stops.campa: Heisenberg returns to Munich to defend a dissertation on the turbulence of fluids, a problem Sommerfeld set him precisely because it lay safely outside quantum controversy. In the oral examination the experimentalist Wilhelm Wien, examining as tradition requires across all of physics, discovers that this celebrated theorist cannot derive the resolving power of a microscope or explain how a storage battery works, and moves to fail him outright. Only Sommerfeld's furious advocacy salvages a bare passing grade; Heisenberg leaves his own doctorate humiliated, and takes the overnight train to Göttingen rather than face his fellow students.
suggested_refs: Heisenberg's doctoral certificate, University of Munich, 1923
sources: APS News, 'The Sad Story of Heisenberg's Doctoral Oral Exam' (1998)

stops.name: Göttingen, the Habilitation
stops.campa: Stung but undeterred, Heisenberg completes his Habilitation under Born within the year, qualifying him at twenty-two to lecture at a German university, and immediately wins a Rockefeller fellowship to study with Bohr in Copenhagen. Born, watching him go, already senses that this student's quarrel with the old quantum theory of orbits and pictures is not a passing rebellion but the shape of a coming revolution, one Born's own Göttingen institute will help to midwife within two more years.
suggested_refs: Heisenberg's Habilitationsschrift, Göttingen, 1924

stops.name: Copenhagen, the Institute on Blegdamsvej
stops.campa: Heisenberg arrives at Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics on Blegdamsvej for a stay of some seven months, drawn into the informal, argumentative, almost familial atmosphere Bohr cultivates among his students, where a half-finished idea can be turned over aloud for hours and no authority stands above correction. He works alongside Hendrik Kramers on the dispersion of light by atoms, a line of calculation treating only frequencies and intensities actually seen in the laboratory, rather than the unobservable orbits behind them, that is quietly preparing the ground for what will break open on a small island the following June.
suggested_refs: The Institute for Theoretical Physics, Blegdamsvej 17, Copenhagen

stops.name: Göttingen, the hay-fever attack
stops.campa: Back in Göttingen, Heisenberg is laid low by a violent attack of hay fever, his face so swollen his colleagues barely recognize him; he asks Born for two weeks' leave and, on a colleague's recommendation, sets out for Helgoland, the one German island reputed to have almost no pollen at all. He arrives exhausted, half-blind with the allergy, carrying with him nothing but the unfinished tangle of calculations, on how to build a theory of the atom from observable transition frequencies and intensities alone, that has consumed him for months.
suggested_refs: Heisenberg's swollen face on arrival, described in Physics and Beyond

stops.name: Helgoland, the treeless rock
stops.campa: On the bare red sandstone island, lodging in a room with a view of the sea and no trees to shed pollen, Heisenberg's fever recedes and his mind clears. Free of lectures, students, and Göttingen's distractions, he throws himself entirely into the arithmetic of atomic transitions, multiplying arrays of numbers standing for spectral-line intensities according to a strange new rule he is inventing as he goes, and finds, again and again, that the scheme does not collapse into contradiction. He climbs the island's rocks in the long June evenings to swim and to think.
suggested_refs: Helgoland's Oberland cliffs, the treeless island of the hay-fever cure

stops.name: Helgoland, the night of the matrices
stops.campa: One night, checking that his new arithmetic conserves energy as it must, Heisenberg finds an error, keeps working past three in the morning, and finally sees the calculation close on itself without contradiction. Trembling with excitement, feeling he is looking clean through the surface of atomic phenomena into a strange and beautiful order beneath, he climbs out to a rock at the island's southern point to watch the sun come up over the sea, too elated to sleep, a twenty-three-year-old certain, and half-frightened by the certainty, that he has found the door into a new mechanics.
stops.quote: I had the feeling that, through the surface of atomic phenomena, I was looking at a strangely beautiful interior, and I felt almost giddy at the thought that I now had to probe this wealth of mathematical structures nature had so generously spread out before me.
stops.quote_source: Werner Heisenberg, Physics and Beyond (1971 English ed.), recounting June 1925
suggested_refs: Lange Anna, the sea stack at Helgoland's southern point, traditional site of the sunrise
sources: AIP.org, 'What Happened on Helgoland' (historians' caution on the memoir's precision)

stops.name: Göttingen, the Drei-Männer-Arbeit
stops.campa: Back in Göttingen, Heisenberg shows his Helgoland paper to Born, who recognizes with a shock that the odd multiplication rule Heisenberg invented from scratch is exactly the algebra of matrices, non-commuting, so that order matters: multiplying A by B is not the same as B by A. Working through the summer and autumn with Born's young assistant Pascual Jordan, the three complete a long joint paper, the Dreimännerarbeit, that turns Heisenberg's single idea into a full mechanics of the atom built entirely from measurable quantities. Quantum theory has, for the first time, a genuine mathematical foundation of its own.
suggested_refs: Born, Heisenberg, Jordan, 'Zur Quantenmechanik II', Zeitschrift für Physik (1925)
sources: Born, Heisenberg, Jordan, Zur Quantenmechanik II (1925)

stops.name: Berlin, the colloquium and Einstein's apartment
stops.campa: Invited to lecture on the new matrix mechanics at the Berlin physics colloquium, Heisenberg meets Albert Einstein for the first time, who afterward walks him home and presses him hard on his own method: is it really sound science to build a theory using only what can be directly observed, and to throw out the electron orbit as a fiction? Heisenberg defends the principle he has just made famous; Einstein answers that it is the theory itself, not raw observation, that decides what can be seen at all, a remark Heisenberg carries unresolved in his mind for the better part of a year, until it resurfaces, transformed, in Copenhagen.
suggested_refs: Einstein's Berlin apartment, Haberlandstrasse 5, Schöneberg
sources: Harvard DASH archive, 'Werner Heisenberg and Albert Einstein'

stops.name: Copenhagen, assistant to Bohr
stops.campa: Heisenberg returns to Copenhagen, now as Bohr's paid lecturer and assistant, sharing lodgings in an attic room of the Institute itself and Bohr's relentless working hours, arguments carried from the seminar room into midnight walks and back again. Erwin Schrödinger's rival wave mechanics has just appeared, mathematically gentler and, to most of the profession's relief, easier to picture; when Schrödinger visits Copenhagen that autumn, Bohr pursues him question by question until, worn out, the older man takes to his bed, Heisenberg continuing the interrogation at his bedside. The two theories will soon be shown equivalent, but the argument over what either of them means is only beginning.
suggested_refs: The attic guest room at the Institute for Theoretical Physics, Copenhagen

stops.name: Copenhagen, the paper while Bohr is skiing
stops.campa: With Bohr away in Norway on a skiing holiday, Heisenberg is left alone at the Institute to think through Einstein's old objection: what, exactly, can be observed. He devises a thought experiment, a gamma-ray microscope trying to fix an electron's position, and shows that the very act of seeing it disturbs its momentum by an amount fixed by Planck's constant: position and momentum can never both be known past a certain joint precision, not from clumsiness but from the nature of measurement itself. He drafts the paper alone, certain he has found something fundamental, before Bohr has even returned from the mountains.
suggested_refs: Heisenberg's gamma-ray microscope thought experiment, 1927
sources: Heisenberg, 'Über den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik', Zeitschrift für Physik (1927)

stops.name: Copenhagen, Bohr's return and complementarity
stops.campa: Bohr comes back from Norway to find the draft finished and is not satisfied: he tells Heisenberg the gamma-ray argument is too narrow, resting on the wave picture of light where it should rest on something deeper, and the two argue so fiercely that Heisenberg is reduced, by his own account, to tears in a Copenhagen stairwell. Bohr's own answer, worked out that same spring, is complementarity: wave and particle, position and momentum, are not rival pictures to be reconciled but two exhaustive descriptions, each valid only within the experimental arrangement that calls it forth. Heisenberg appends Bohr's correction to the printed paper; the uncertainty principle leaves Copenhagen changed by the argument that named it.
suggested_refs: The appended note on complementarity, Heisenberg's 1927 uncertainty paper
sources: AIP History: 'Triumph of the Copenhagen Interpretation'

stops.name: Brussels, the Fifth Solvay Conference
stops.campa: At the Solvay Conference in Brussels, the world's assembled quantum physicists gather for the photograph now famous in every physics classroom, and behind it the real argument begins: Bohr and Einstein across the dinner table, Einstein constructing overnight a new thought experiment meant to defeat the uncertainty principle, Bohr demolishing it again each following morning, sometimes with Einstein's own relativity turned against him. Heisenberg and Pauli, watching from the younger ranks, come away convinced complementarity has survived every attack intact; Einstein, unconvinced to the end of his life, mutters privately that God does not play dice.
suggested_refs: The 1927 Solvay Conference photograph, Institut International de Physique Solvay

stops.name: Leipzig, the professor at twenty-six
stops.campa: Leipzig calls Heisenberg to its chair of theoretical physics, and at twenty-five he becomes the youngest full professor in Germany, younger than some of the doctoral students who will soon fill his seminar room. He designs the institute to run on Bohr's Copenhagen model, argument and openness rather than hierarchy, and within a few years it rivals Göttingen and Copenhagen themselves as a forge of the new physics, drawing students from across Europe eager to work under the man who built matrix mechanics before he was old enough, by German custom, to be fully believed.
suggested_refs: Heisenberg's Institute for Theoretical Physics, Leipzig University

stops.name: Leipzig, the school
stops.campa: Rudolf Peierls, Felix Bloch, Edward Teller, Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker, Victor Weisskopf: the roll of students who pass through Heisenberg's Leipzig seminar in these years reads, in time, like a roster of the century's physics, scattered by what is coming into every camp of the war soon to follow. He works now on ferromagnetism, on the quantum theory of the atomic nucleus once Chadwick's neutron is found in 1932, and on cosmic rays, restless as ever to move to the next unopened door once a first one has been forced.
suggested_refs: Group photographs of the Leipzig school, early 1930s

stops.name: Stockholm, the Nobel ceremony
stops.campa: The Nobel committee, having found no worthy laureate for 1932, awards Heisenberg that year's prize in physics 'for the creation of quantum mechanics' together with the delayed 1933 prizes to Schrödinger and Dirac, and the three share the Stockholm ceremony before the Swedish court. Heisenberg is thirty-one, already for six years the youngest full professor in the country he is going home to, a Germany where, in this same month, the National Socialist state is not yet a year old and tightening around the university world he has built his whole life inside.
suggested_refs: The Nobel Prize in Physics 1932 medal and diploma, awarded 1933
sources: Nobel Prize in Physics 1932, official citation and ceremony speech

segments.name: The White Jew: Shadows over German Physics

stops.name: Leipzig, marriage to Elisabeth Schumacher
stops.campa: At a private musical evening in Leipzig, Heisenberg meets Elisabeth Schumacher; they are engaged within two weeks and married within four months, on the twenty-ninth of April, a whirlwind unlike anything in his cautious professional life. She is the daughter of a well-connected Berlin economist, quick-tongued and unintimidated by her husband's fame, and will become, in the correspondence they keep through the coming war years, the one steady confidante to whom he writes what he can tell almost no one at the Institute.
suggested_refs: Werner and Elisabeth Heisenberg's wedding photograph, Leipzig, 1937
'My Dear Li', the published wartime correspondence
sources: Elisabeth Heisenberg correspondence, published as My Dear Li (2011 English ed.)

stops.name: Munich, "weisse Juden" in Das Schwarze Korps
stops.campa: As Heisenberg travels toward Munich hoping to succeed the retired Sommerfeld in his old chair, the SS weekly Das Schwarze Korps publishes a full-page denunciation, engineered by the physicist Johannes Stark, naming him a 'white Jew', a German who spreads the Jewish spirit of 'relativity and Bohr's atomic mysticism' though not Jewish by blood, and declaring that men like him must 'disappear' from German science as the Jews themselves are being made to disappear. The chair goes instead to a proponent of the regime's 'German Physics'; for months Heisenberg does not know whether the attack will cost him his career, or worse.
suggested_refs: Das Schwarze Korps, front page, 15 July 1937, '"Weisse Juden" in der Wissenschaft'

stops.name: Berlin, Himmler's letter
stops.campa: Heisenberg's mother, through an old family connection, calls on Himmler's mother, one boy's welfare pleaded to another; Heisenberg himself is summoned to the SS headquarters on the Prinz-Albrecht-Strasse for a night of interrogation before he is allowed to go. More than a year after the article, Himmler personally writes to clear him of the charge, on the condition, as Heisenberg understands it, that he keep his physics and his public silence strictly separate from now on: he may go on teaching relativity and the new mechanics, but he is to stop naming the men, many of them Jewish, who built it.
stops.quote: I have looked at your case very carefully, and thought it necessary to write you these lines as I do not approve of the attack against you in the Schwarze Korps.
stops.quote_source: Heinrich Himmler to Werner Heisenberg, letter of 21 July 1938
suggested_refs: Himmler's letter to Heisenberg, 21 July 1938, Deutsches Museum archive

stops.name: Leipzig, news of fission
stops.campa: Word reaches Leipzig of Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann's discovery in Berlin, published in January: bombarded with neutrons, the uranium nucleus does not merely absorb them but splits nearly in two, releasing an energy that Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch, in exile, are first to explain correctly as fission. Heisenberg reads the paper with the rest of German physics and understands at once, as every capable nuclear physicist in Europe and America understands within weeks, that a chain reaction, and conceivably a weapon, now lies somewhere down the road this single laboratory result has opened.
suggested_refs: Hahn and Strassmann, 'Über den Nachweis...', Naturwissenschaften (January 1939)

segments.name: The Uranverein: War and the Bomb that Wasn't

stops.name: Berlin, the Army Ordnance Office and the Uranverein
stops.campa: Within weeks of the war's outbreak, Heisenberg is drafted into the Army Ordnance Office's new Uranverein, the uranium research group assessing whether fission can be turned to military use. He writes the group's first theoretical reports on the physics of a chain reaction and a possible reactor, calculating, correctly, that natural uranium moderated by heavy water or graphite could sustain one; on the harder question of an actual bomb, requiring uranium enriched or transmuted to a critical mass most in Germany believe unreachable in wartime, his own reckoning stays, for now, unfinished.
suggested_refs: Heisenberg's Uranverein report, 'Die Möglichkeit der technischen Energiegewinnung aus der Uranspaltung' (1939)
sources: Mark Walker, German National Socialism and the Quest for Nuclear Power (1989)

stops.name: Copenhagen, the visit to Bohr
stops.campa: Heisenberg travels to occupied Copenhagen ostensibly to lecture at the German cultural institute, and arranges, against the discomfort of Danish colleagues who now shun all contact with the occupier's representatives, a private meeting with Bohr, his teacher of twenty years. What passes between them alone is never agreed upon again: Heisenberg will later say he raised, obliquely, whether a physicist has the moral right to work toward atomic weapons at all, hoping to sound out an understanding between the two camps; Bohr comes away convinced his former student was confirming a German bomb program already confident of success. They part within the hour, and never resume the old friendship.
stops.quote: One may perhaps ask whether the physicists have the moral right to work on the practical exploitation of atomic energy at all.
stops.quote_source: Heisenberg's postwar account of his own words to Bohr, recalled in Physics and Beyond (1971); disputed in Bohr's unsent 1957 draft letters
suggested_refs: Niels Bohr's residence of honour, the Carlsberg mansion, Copenhagen
The Niels Bohr Archive's released Bohr-Heisenberg documents (2002)

stops.name: Berlin-Dahlem, the Harnack Haus briefing
stops.campa: Called before Albert Speer, Hitler's new armaments minister, and the heads of the army and air force at the Kaiser Wilhelm Society's Harnack House, Heisenberg and his fellow physicists are asked directly what a bomb would require and when. He answers honestly that a weapon lies years beyond Germany's wartime reach, though a power-producing reactor is close; Speer, hearing no prospect of a decisive weapon before the war's likely end, assigns the uranium project a modest budget and a low priority next to rockets and jets, a verdict that spares the group the kind of forced, all-consuming effort the Manhattan Project is, at that same hour, just beginning in America.
suggested_refs: Harnack House, Berlin-Dahlem, site of the 4 June 1942 briefing
sources: Harnack Haus historical archive, Max Planck Society

stops.name: Haigerloch, the reactor in the rock cellar
stops.campa: As Allied bombing flattens Berlin, Heisenberg's group moves its last reactor experiment to Haigerloch, a small Swabian town, and builds it inside a rock-cut cellar beneath the church, hanging six hundred and sixty-four cubes of uranium metal on cables in a tank of heavy water. Through March they inch the pile's multiplication factor upward without ever quite reaching the self-sustaining chain reaction Heisenberg's own theory says lies just a little further off, lacking, in the end, only more uranium and more heavy water than the collapsing Reich can any longer supply. Nine days before American troops seize the site, work stops for good.
suggested_refs: The Atomkeller, Haigerloch's rock-cut reactor cellar, now a museum
sources: Walker, German National Socialism and the Quest for Nuclear Power (1989)

stops.name: Urfeld am Walchensee, the capture
stops.campa: With the reactor group's records and remaining uranium buried in a field and a latrine at Haigerloch for American hands to find, Heisenberg cycles alone across a collapsing Bavaria, through territory still held by SS units executing deserters, to reach his family at their lake house above the Walchensee. Within days Colonel Boris Pash's Alsos mission, hunting the last of the Uranverein physicists, finds him there and takes him into custody; within the week he and the rest of the German nuclear team are in American hands and bound, by way of France and Belgium, for an English country house whose existence none of them yet suspects.
suggested_refs: The Heisenberg family's summer house, Urfeld am Walchensee

stops.name: Farm Hall, Godmanchester
stops.campa: Ten German physicists, Heisenberg, Hahn, Weizsäcker, Gerlach, Diebner, Bagge, Wirtz, Korsching, von Laue, and Harteck, are interned together at Farm Hall, a Georgian country house near Godmanchester, ostensibly as comfortable house guests and in fact as intelligence subjects: every room is wired, and a British team transcribes their conversations around the clock. Unaware of the microphones, the men debate physics, politics, and their own conduct under Hitler with each other more openly than they have dared with anyone in twelve years, producing, without their knowledge, the single most candid record of what German nuclear physicists actually believed they had, and had not, achieved.
suggested_refs: Farm Hall, Godmanchester, Huntingdonshire, the listening house
Operation Epsilon: The Farm Hall Transcripts (1993, ed. Jeremy Bernstein)
sources: Operation Epsilon: The Farm Hall Transcripts (1993)

stops.name: Farm Hall, the news from Hiroshima
stops.campa: At six o'clock the BBC evening news reports that an American atomic bomb has destroyed the Japanese city of Hiroshima. Heisenberg's first reaction, overheard by the hidden microphones, is blank disbelief: he cannot credit that the Americans, and the other physicist he has never met, Oppenheimer, found the route to a bomb this fast, and says so flatly to the room. Hahn, who discovered fission in the first place, is devastated, confesses he had thought at times of taking his own life rather than have this weapon made from his discovery, and is given whisky and reassured by his colleagues that he personally bears no guilt for how others used what he found.
stops.quote: I don't believe a word of the whole thing.
stops.quote_source: Farm Hall transcripts, Operation Epsilon, evening of 6 August 1945
suggested_refs: The recorded transcript of the evening of 6 August 1945, Farm Hall
sources: Operation Epsilon: The Farm Hall Transcripts (1993, ed. Bernstein)

stops.name: Farm Hall, the lecture he could not quite finish
stops.campa: Over the following days Heisenberg works alone in his room and then, before the others, attempts to reconstruct on paper how the American bomb must actually have been built, only to arrive, in his first pass, at a critical mass calculation wildly too large to be practical, an error the war years of half-resourced, unpressured work had never forced him to correct. He revises it within a fortnight to something closer to the true figure, reasoning the problem through properly for the first time in his life, a private, recorded demonstration, to historians ever since, of how far German bomb physics genuinely got, and did not get, under his direction.
suggested_refs: Heisenberg's corrected critical-mass lecture, Farm Hall, mid-August 1945
sources: Operation Epsilon: The Farm Hall Transcripts (1993)

segments.name: Göttingen to Munich: the Long Coda

stops.name: Göttingen, director of the Max Planck Institute
stops.campa: Released from Farm Hall and returned to a defeated, divided Germany, Heisenberg takes up the directorship of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics, refounded within the year as the Max Planck Institute, in Göttingen, and sets himself to the unglamorous work of rebuilding German physics from occupation-zone rubble: scavenging equipment, training a generation with no living memory of the field's prewar glories, arguing for civilian nuclear research under Allied restriction. He writes, in these same years, the first drafts of the memoir and the popular philosophy that will occupy much of his remaining public life, an accounting, oblique and unfinished, of what the preceding decade had actually meant.
suggested_refs: The Max Planck Institute for Physics, Göttingen, refounded 1946
sources: Max Planck Institute for Physics, institutional history

stops.name: Göttingen, the Manifesto of the Eighteen
stops.campa: When Chancellor Adenauer's government proposes arming the new Bundeswehr with tactical nuclear weapons, Heisenberg joins seventeen other leading West German physicists, Hahn, Born, von Laue, Weizsäcker among them, in signing the Göttingen Manifesto, declaring that none of them will take part in the production, testing, or deployment of any nuclear weapon whatever. It is as close as Heisenberg ever comes to a public verdict on the year he spent building reactors for the government he once served; the ambiguity of Farm Hall is not explained here, only, at last, closed off going forward.
stops.quote: We believe that a small country such as the Federal Republic best protects itself and secures peace in the world today by renouncing possession of nuclear weapons of every kind.
stops.quote_source: The Göttingen Manifesto, signed jointly by Heisenberg and seventeen others, 12 April 1957
suggested_refs: The Göttingen Manifesto, original signed text, 12 April 1957
sources: Max Planck Society, 'Scientists unite for peace' retrospective

stops.name: Munich, the Institute moves, the world formula
stops.campa: The Max Planck Institute for Physics relocates to Munich, and Heisenberg with it, back to the city of his schooldays; that same year he publishes Physics and Philosophy, his account for a general readership of what quantum theory had actually done to the idea of an observer-independent world. With Pauli he also pursues, and briefly announces to the press, a unified 'world formula' meant to derive every elementary particle from a single nonlinear spinor equation; Pauli's enthusiasm curdles within months into open scorn, the two men's decades-old friendship strained by a theory that will not, in the end, survive either man's lifetime.
suggested_refs: Heisenberg, Physics and Philosophy: The Revolution in Modern Science (1958)
The unified 'world formula' equation, announced 1958
sources: Charles Enz, No Time to Be Brief: A Scientific Biography of Wolfgang Pauli (2002)

stops.name: Munich, the memoir and the last years
stops.campa: In his final two decades Heisenberg serves as president of the Alexander von Humboldt Foundation, campaigns for European scientific cooperation, and publishes Der Teil und das Ganze, Physics and Beyond in English, his memoir told as a sequence of remembered conversations, Sommerfeld, Bohr, Einstein, Bohr again at Copenhagen in 1941, in which he lets the reader watch him think without ever quite rendering a final verdict on the bomb years. He dies of cancer in his Munich home on the first of February, seventy-four years old, the uncertainty he found on a treeless island fifty-one years before by then one of the fixed foundations of physics itself.
suggested_refs: Heisenberg, Der Teil und das Ganze / Physics and Beyond (1969)
Heisenberg's grave, Munich Waldfriedhof
sources: Heisenberg, Physics and Beyond / Der Teil und das Ganze (1969)
